claims.text: The compared Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
Mechanical behavior depends on the identities and combinations of constituent elements, not merely on constituent count.
Specific elemental combinations modify local lattice distortions.
Specific elemental combinations modify stacking-fault energy.
Balanced multicomponent interactions in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni produce a uniform distribution of lattice distortions.
The proposed uniform lattice-distortion distribution favors controlled dislocation slip.
Removing constituents from the quinary alloy disrupts the proposed balance of multicomponent interactions.
Disruption of the proposed interaction balance alters dislocation dynamics and deformation and failure behavior.
Local lattice distortions cause changes in stacking-fault energy.
Changes in stacking-fault energy influence dislocation-core structures.
Changes in stacking-fault energy influence slip-system activation.
The quinary alloy has an optimum stacking-fault energy that facilitates dislocation glide.
The proposed optimum stacking-fault energy facilitates controlled strain hardening in the quinary alloy.
Altered solute interactions in the quaternary and ternary alloys change slip-system activation.
Changed slip-system activation in the reduced-composition alloys can cause premature strain localization or an altered yield response.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will show a strength-ductility tradeoff, although the direction of the difference is not specified.
The reduced-composition alloys are expected to exhibit lower uniform elongation than the quinary alloy.
Differences in yield strength, uniform elongation, and strain hardening should correlate with differences in stacking-fault energy and local lattice distortion.
The proposed controlled comparison uses identically processed quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys tested at the same room temperature and strain rate.
The hypothesis is restricted to alloys that remain single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing and are tested under matched environmental conditions.
